summary: Describes the transport of syslog messages over UDP on IPv4 or IPv6. Implementations of the syslog protocol are required to support this mapping so they can interoperate. This is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: This is the simplest way to mail diary entries: drop each one in the mailbox without waiting for a reply. It's quick, but a few might get lost.

questions: how big can a syslog udp message be
subtitle: The mandatory-to-implement way to carry syslog messages in single UDP datagrams, and what that costs you.

tldr.problem: The syslog protocol allows many transport mappings, but implementations need at least one common transport to interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: Each syslog message goes in its own UDP datagram over IPv4 or IPv6, sent to UDP port 514, with minimum receive sizes of 480 octets for IPv4 and 1180 octets for IPv6.
tldr.outcome: It is lightweight but unreliable and insecure: no loss detection, no congestion control, no authentication. The TLS transport is the recommended choice outside managed networks.

today: RFC 5426 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself points to the TLS transport (RFC 5425) as the one to use outside managed networks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Informational RFC 3164 described syslog as observed in existing implementations, including both the message format and a UDP transport. A Standards-Track syslog protocol was later defined in RFC 5424, which uses a layered architecture that allows any number of transport mappings.

RFC 5426 describes the UDP transport mapping, usable over both IPv4 and IPv6. For interoperability, syslog implementers are required to support it. The RFC warns that administrators should know about its significant reliability and security issues, which stem from UDP. It is lightweight and builds on the existing popular use of UDP for syslog.
sections.eli5: Syslog is how computers write down what is happening. This RFC says how to send those notes using the simplest delivery method, which is fast but a bit careless.

sections.title: One Message Per Datagram
sections.content:
Each syslog UDP datagram MUST contain only one syslog message. The message MAY be complete or truncated, MUST be formatted and truncated according to RFC 5424, and no additional data may be present in the datagram payload.

The datagram must follow the structure in the UDP RFC (RFC 768) and either the IPv4 RFC 791 or the IPv6 RFC 2460, depending on which protocol is used.
sections.eli5: One envelope holds exactly one note, and nothing else goes inside.

sections.title: Message Size and Ports
sections.content:
Messages can be up to 65535 octets minus the UDP header length, a limit that comes from the maximum UDP size in RFC 768. For IPv4 the IP header is subtracted as well.

The interoperability baseline is: IPv4 receivers MUST accept messages up to and including 480 octets, IPv6 receivers MUST accept up to 1180 octets, and all receivers SHOULD accept up to 2048 octets. Larger is encouraged. These come from the minimum MTU hosts must support, 576 octets for IPv4 and 1280 octets for IPv6, so conforming datagrams avoid fragmentation.

Senders are RECOMMENDED to keep IP datagrams within the smallest MTU of the network in use. Fragmentation raises the risk of loss, since losing one fragment loses the message. Syslog has no acknowledgements, so it cannot use packetization layer path MTU discovery. When the MTU is unknown, the safest assumption is 480 octets for IPv4 and 1180 octets for IPv6.

On ports, receivers MUST accept syslog datagrams on well-known UDP port 514 and senders MUST support sending to it. Both MAY be configurable to use another port, and senders MAY use any source port.
sections.eli5: Small notes get there most safely, because big ones get cut into pieces and losing one piece ruins the note. Everyone listens at the same mailbox number, 514.

sections.title: Source Address and Checksums
sections.content:
The source IP address of the datagram SHOULD NOT be treated as the identifier of the host that originated the message, because the sender could merely be a relay. The syslog message itself carries the originator's identifier.

Senders MUST NOT disable UDP checksums, and IPv4 senders SHOULD use them. IPv4 receivers SHOULD check checksums and SHOULD accept a message with a zero checksum. Receivers MUST NOT disable checksum checks. For IPv6, RFC 2460 already mandates UDP checksums.
sections.eli5: The return address on the envelope may just be a post office that passed it along, so read the name written inside the note instead.

sections.title: Reliability Considerations
sections.content:
UDP is an unreliable, low-overhead protocol, and this mapping adds nothing to fix that.

  • Lost datagrams: there is no mechanism to detect or correct loss. Fragmentation makes it worse because one lost fragment discards the whole message.
  • Corruption: UDP checksums help detect it, but they do not guarantee detection, and there is no acknowledgement or retransmission.
  • Congestion control: syslog can generate unlimited data and UDP has no congestion control, so the TLS transport (RFC 5425) is REQUIRED to implement and RECOMMENDED for general use. UDP syslog MAY be used instead only in managed networks provisioned for it, for example through rate limiting or capacity reservations.
  • Ordering: delivery order may differ from send order. Message time stamps are a rough guide, but arrival order SHOULD NOT be used as an authoritative sequence of events.
sections.eli5: Notes can get lost, damaged or arrive out of order, and nobody tells you. So for important mail, use the safer service.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Using this specification on an unsecured network is NOT RECOMMENDED. Some issues can be mitigated with IPsec (RFC 4301). The RFC lists these concerns:

  • Forgery and weak sender authentication: a receiver cannot tell whether a message really came from the reported sender. An attacker can bury a real attack under forged alarms, or forge a notice that a stopped process had restarted.
  • Observation: messages are not confidential in transit. No sensitive information should be sent this way, or only over properly secured networks.
  • Replay: recorded normal-looking messages could be replayed with new time stamps.
  • Unreliable delivery: lost messages can hide a developing problem, and an attacker could discard messages deliberately.
  • Prioritization: nothing mandates severity-based priority, so floods of low-severity messages could push out high-severity ones.
  • Denial of service: a receiver can be overwhelmed. Implementers SHOULD provide features such as optionally restricting reception to known source IP addresses.
sections.eli5: Anyone can write a fake note, read the notes, or throw them away. So do not send secrets this way, and prefer a locked mailbox when it matters.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: This transport uses UDP port 514 for syslog, as recorded in the IANA port-numbers registry. The RFC asks IANA for nothing new.
sections.eli5: Port 514 is already written down in the official list of port numbers.

items.label: IPv4 receivers
items.desc: MUST receive messages up to and including 480 octets.

items.label: IPv6 receivers
items.desc: MUST receive messages up to and including 1180 octets.

items.label: All receivers
items.desc: SHOULD receive messages up to and including 2048 octets.
